title: Why Be Original?
use_cases: Use when planning narrative twists to ensure they serve a strategic purpose
Implement when evaluating if a manuscript aligns with specific genre requirements
Configure when balancing familiar story frameworks with original element delivery
Use when seeking to increase reader engagement and post-reading recommendations
content:
Before we look at how to turn things on their heads, you should understand that it is still necessary for authors to follow or meet reader expectations most of the time—at least for the big, important ones. Structure and certain plot points or beats are essential and provide a familiar framework for readers, allowing them to navigate the story easily.

Certain tropes or parameters are also required for your manuscript to fit within your chosen genre. For example, your cozy mystery with a career detective solving a gruesome crime isn’t subverting expectations. Your manuscript is simply not that subgenre anymore. If you twist something for your reader, you need to do so intentionally and strategically.

When done well, the techniques used to subvert reader expectations can be of great benefit to a novel. When you surprise a reader in a good way, your book sticks in their mind. They’ll recommend it to friends and take the time to leave a review. But a novel that’s too predictable or littered with clichés will soon be forgotten.

To properly mix things up, you need to watch your frequency of employing this writing technique—i.e., is it twist after twist after twist in a few short pages? And you need to ensure you have a purpose for each topsy-turvy moment. Here are a few ways you can work to subvert reader expectations in your book.
